column3: Four unicellular or simple eukaryotic preparations have these features: P has a flexible pellicle and can photosynthesise in light but use organic food in darkness; Q has a wall made of two overlapping silica-rich halves; R has cellulose plates and two differently oriented flagella; S forms a multinucleate feeding mass and later spore-bearing fruiting structures. Which ordered assignment is consistent?
column4: P euglenoid; Q diatom; R dinoflagellate; S slime mould
column5: P diatom; Q euglenoid; R slime mould; S dinoflagellate
column6: P dinoflagellate; Q slime mould; R diatom; S euglenoid
column7: P slime mould; Q dinoflagellate; R euglenoid; S diatom
column9:
Answer: (A) Euglenoid, diatom, dinoflagellate and slime mould.
Why: P combines a flexible covering with condition-dependent nutritional modes typical of euglenoids. Q's two-part siliceous wall is diagnostic of diatoms, whereas R's plates and flagellar arrangement fit dinoflagellates. S's feeding plasmodial mass and subsequent spore-bearing structures distinguish the slime-mould life form. All four observations must agree with the assignment; photosynthesis alone would not separate the first three groups.
Why not the others: (B) swaps the pellicle and siliceous-wall organisms and assigns the plasmodial stage to dinoflagellates. (C) gives the silica wall to a slime mould and places the flagellar plates in a diatom. (D) assigns a flexible photosynthetic cell to the plasmodial group and reverses the other diagnostic coverings.
Key point: Use covering, movement and life-cycle evidence together instead of classifying a protist by nutrition alone.
column10: Four protist groups separated by coverings, flagella and a feeding-to-spore transition

column3: Both underground structures P and Q in the figure store food. P has repeated nodes with scale leaves and axillary buds; Q bears lateral roots but has no nodes or leaf-associated buds. Which inference follows from the structural evidence rather than their shared storage function?
column4: P and Q are both roots because they grow below ground
column5: P is a modified stem and Q a modified root
column6: P is a modified root and Q a modified stem
column7: P and Q must be leaves because they contain stored carbohydrate
column9:
Answer: (B) P is a modified stem and Q a modified root.
Why: Nodes, scale leaves and axillary buds belong to the shoot organisation and identify P as a modified stem despite its underground position. Q lacks those features and has the stated root organisation. Storage is a function that can be performed by different organs, so neither the shared function nor location overrides the morphological evidence.
Why not the others: (A) treats underground position as a sufficient root character. (C) reverses the significance of nodes and axillary buds. (D) confuses the chemical contents of an organ with its developmental identity.
Key point: Determine organ identity from its structural markers before using its location or function.
column10: Nodes and buds identify an underground stem despite a root-like storage role
column11: Morphology of flowering plants: The Root; The Stem; Modifications

column3: A stipulated eukaryotic chromatin model contains 6000 bp of DNA in identical 200 bp repeats. Each repeat has one core of eight histone molecules, with 146 bp wrapped around that core and the rest as linker DNA. Ignore end effects and linker histone H1. How many core histone molecules and how many linker base pairs are present?
column9:
Answer: (C) 240 core histone molecules and 1620 linker bp.
Given: Total DNA 6000 bp; repeat 200 bp; eight core histones and 146 wrapped bp per repeat.
Formula/Principle: Count repeats first, then distinguish core protein count from unwrapped DNA amount.
Step 1: \[N_{m repeat}=6000/200=30.\]
Step 2: \[N_{m histone}=30(8)=240	ext{ molecules}.\]
Step 3: Linker length per repeat is \(200-146=54\) bp, so \[L_{m linker}=30(54)=1620	ext{ bp}.\]
Why: The core is an octamer, not one histone molecule, while a repeat includes both wrapped and linker DNA. The two requested quantities therefore use different multipliers after the same repeat count. Packaging the DNA does not cut away the linker or change the base-pair total.
Why not the others: (A) counts cores instead of histone molecules. (B) reports the wrapped DNA length rather than the linker length. (D) doubles both counts as though a base pair were two independent repeats.
Key point: Keep structural-unit count, protein stoichiometry and DNA length in separate accounts.
column10: Chromatin repeat length distinguishes core histone count from linker DNA
column11: Molecular basis of inheritance: Packaging of DNA Helix; Cell: Nucleus

column3: Mature plant parenchyma cells rarely divide in their original tissue. In a supplied culture medium they resume division and form callus. Transfer of that callus to a different growth-regulator mixture produces organised shoots. No DNA-sequence change is detected. Which interpretation is best supported?
column4: The first transition includes dedifferentiation; the second includes redifferentiation under changed regulatory conditions
column5: The callus must have lost all capacity to differentiate because it divided
column6: Shoot formation proves a new mutation created every developmental instruction
column7: The original cells completed meiosis and became gametes before forming shoots
column9:
Answer: (A) Dedifferentiation followed by redifferentiation.
Why: Previously differentiated cells regaining proliferative capacity illustrate dedifferentiation. Their descendants then acquiring organised shoot characteristics illustrate redifferentiation. Changing the hormonal environment can regulate which existing developmental capacities are expressed without requiring a new DNA sequence for every tissue type. The experiment therefore separates a change of cellular state from a required mutational explanation.
Why not the others: (D) introduces a reduction division and gametic stage not observed in the tissue culture. (B) contradicts the later formation of organised shoots. (C) treats a regulated developmental response as proof of mutations despite the stated sequence evidence.
Key point: A cell can change developmental state and fate through regulation without acquiring a new genome.
column10: Regulator-dependent proliferation and organ formation separate dedifferentiation from redifferentiation
column11: Plant growth and development: Differentiation; Dedifferentiation; Redifferentiation; Plant Growth Regulators

column3: In an idealised central-nervous-system comparison, intervention X disrupts balance and coordination of voluntary movements while basic breathing rhythm remains. Intervention Y disrupts the normal breathing rhythm while skeletal muscles can still contract when stimulated. Which affected regions are most consistent with X and Y, respectively?
column4: Spinal sensory roots and cerebral motor cortex
column9:
Answer: (D) Cerebellum and medulla oblongata.
Why: The cerebellum contributes to coordination, precision and balance, so impaired coordination need not mean the muscles themselves cannot produce force. The medulla contains important centres controlling respiratory rhythm; muscle contractility does not substitute for that coordinated neural drive. Preserved breathing in X and preserved direct muscle responses in Y help separate coordination and rhythm control from a general failure of all motor tissue. These are idealised functional assignments, not a unique clinical diagnosis from two symptoms.
Why not the others: (B) exchanges the main coordination and respiratory-rhythm assignments. (C) does not match the stated coordination role in X and confuses loss of respiratory drive with a necessary loss of muscle contractility. (A) substitutes peripheral sensory interruption for the given central coordination comparison.
Key point: Distinguish the ability of an effector to respond from the central organisation of its activity.
column10: Preserved effectors distinguish movement coordination from central respiratory-rhythm control
column11: Neural control and coordination: Central Neural System; Cerebellum; Medulla

column3: Developing pollen loses viability after a treatment damages the anther's nutritive inner wall layer. Moving that pollen to several otherwise compatible stigmas does not restore germination. Separate chemical treatment leaves the pollen exine resistant while removing other wall material. Which pair of assignments fits the two observations?
column4: The damaged layer is the stigma; the resistant wall material is cellulose
column5: The damaged layer is the tapetum; the resistant material is sporopollenin
column6: The damaged layer is the ovule integument; the resistant material is pectin
column7: The damaged layer is the endosperm; the resistant material is lignin
column9:
Answer: (B) Tapetum and sporopollenin.
Why: The tapetum is the nutritive anther layer associated with developing pollen, so damage before pollen maturation can impair pollen regardless of which compatible stigma later receives it. Sporopollenin accounts for the remarkable resistance of the exine. The stigma-transfer result places the defect before a particular pollen-stigma compatibility interaction, while the chemical-resistance result identifies a different structural feature of pollen.
Why not the others: (A) locates the original treatment in a receptive female surface rather than the stated anther layer and replaces the resistant exine polymer by a different wall component. (C) concerns an ovule tissue and a non-exine wall material. (D) assigns a post-fertilisation nutritive tissue to anther development and substitutes lignin for sporopollenin.
Key point: Use the developmental location of a defect separately from the chemical identity of a protective wall.
column10: Anther nutrition failure and exine chemical resistance provide independent pollen evidence
column11: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants: Pre-fertilisation Structures and Events; Microsporangium; Pollen

column3: A mother's X chromosomes bear centromere-linked markers XA and Xa; the father's chromosomes are XB and Y. Assume no crossing over between each marker and its centromere and no post-zygotic chromosome change. In separate conceptions, two XXY children have complements XA-Xa-Y and XA-XA-Y. Which maternal nondisjunction stages most directly account for the first and second complements?
column9:
Answer: (C) Maternal meiosis I and maternal meiosis II.
Why: Failure to separate homologous maternal X chromosomes in meiosis I can retain both different centromeric markers in one egg. After a normal meiosis-I separation, failure of sister chromatids to separate in meiosis II can instead give an egg with two copies bearing the same marker. Fertilisation by a Y-bearing sperm gives the stated XXY complements. The absence of paternal XB from both children, together with the stated exclusions, localises the extra X material to the maternal route. The centromere/no-recombination condition is necessary because distal recombination could otherwise obscure the sister-versus-homologue marker distinction.
Why not the others: (A) reverses retention of different homologues and duplicate sisters. (B) cannot explain the identical marker pair in the second child under the given assumptions. (D) cannot retain both different maternal centromeric markers in the first child after normal homologue separation.
Key point: Centromere-linked heterozygosity versus duplicate sister markers can distinguish which meiotic separation failed.
column10: Maternal centromeric marker identity separates meiosis-I from meiosis-II nondisjunction
column11: Principles of inheritance and variation: Chromosomal Disorders; Sex Determination; Cell Division

column3: Product P from Monascus purpureus competitively inhibits an enzyme in cholesterol synthesis. Product Q from Trichoderma polysporum suppresses immune responses. Which industrial-product assignments match these distinct targets?
column9:
Answer: (D) Statin and cyclosporin A.
Why: Monascus-derived statins are associated with inhibition of cholesterol synthesis, whereas cyclosporin A from Trichoderma polysporum is used for its immunosuppressive action. The target evidence distinguishes these products from antibacterial agents and clot-dissolving enzymes even though all may be discussed among useful microbial products. Being produced by a fungus does not make every product an antibiotic or give it the same cellular target.
Why not the others: (A) replaces the cholesterol-synthesis inhibitor by an antibacterial drug and the immunosuppressant by a clot-dissolving enzyme. (B) reverses the two target-specific assignments. (C) misassigns both the clot-dissolving and antibacterial products to the stated activities.
Key point: Identify a microbial product by its source and biological target rather than assuming a shared source implies a shared action.
column10: Two fungal industrial products distinguished by enzyme inhibition versus immunosuppression
column11: Microbes in human welfare: Microbes in Industrial Products

column3: In a stipulated ADA-deficiency gene-therapy model, functional ADA cDNA is introduced into a patient's lymphocytes, which are returned to the patient. The corrected cells make ADA but have limited persistence. Which change would most directly address the need for repeated cell infusions, if feasible?
column4: Introduce a persistent corrected progenitor population that can keep supplying functional descendants
column5: Remove the functional cDNA immediately after the lymphocytes enter the blood
column6: Use uncorrected lymphocytes because their normal life span is longer than the cDNA sequence
column7: Keep the same short-lived corrected cells but assume their temporary enzyme production permanently changes every other cell's genome
column9:
Answer: (A) A persistent corrected progenitor population.
Why: Enzyme production in the returned lymphocytes can be functional yet temporary because those cells do not persist indefinitely. A suitably corrected self-renewing or persistent source of descendants addresses that cellular limitation rather than merely increasing one transient enzyme pulse. The conclusion is a mechanism within the stated model, not a claim that every clinical gene-therapy procedure automatically cures the disorder.
Why not the others: (B) removes the genetic instruction responsible for restored enzyme production. (C) supplies cells that still lack the corrected function and gives an unsupported lifespan comparison. (D) assumes secreted or cellular enzyme activity rewrites unrelated genomes, which does not follow.
Key point: Distinguish successful gene expression in a short-lived cell from persistence of a corrected cell lineage.
column10: Limited corrected-cell persistence motivates a progenitor-level gene-therapy strategy
column11: Biotechnology and its application: Biotechnological Applications in Medicine; Gene Therapy

column3: A wasp pollinates a fig and its larvae consume some developing seeds. Measurements show that the tree produces more viable seeds with the wasp than without it, and the wasp completes reproduction only in this interaction. Which interpretation is consistent with the evidence at both scales?
column4: The interaction must be parasitism at every scale because at least one seed is eaten
column5: The measured whole-organism interaction can be mutualistic despite a cost to individual consumed seeds
column6: The tree must receive no benefit because the wasp reproduces
column7: Mutualism requires that neither partner use any material or energy supplied by the other
column9:
Answer: (B) A net mutualistic interaction can include individual seed costs.
Why: The measured increase in viable-seed production establishes a reproductive benefit to the tree under the comparison, while the wasp gains a required reproductive opportunity. Consumption of some seeds is a real local cost, but it does not erase the larger measured net benefit. Interaction labels therefore depend on the partner-level outcomes being assessed; a mutualistic relationship need not mean that every component of each organism is unharmed.
Why not the others: (A) treats one local cost as sufficient to reverse both measured net outcomes. (C) assumes one partner's reproduction excludes benefit to the other. (D) wrongly excludes the resource exchanges that often enable mutualism.
Key point: Evaluate net partner outcomes at the stated scale before naming a population interaction.
column10: A seed-level cost coexists with a measured mutualistic partner-level outcome
column11: Organisms and populations: Population Interactions; Mutualism

column3: Inherited disorder P reduces production of an otherwise ordinary globin-chain type. In disorder Q, a beta-globin amino-acid substitution promotes abnormal haemoglobin behaviour and red-cell sickling under low oxygen. Which distinction is most consistent with these observations?
column4: P is a qualitative haemoglobin change; Q is only a reduction in chain amount
column5: P and Q must both be caused solely by dietary iron deficiency
column6: P fits a quantitative thalassaemia defect; Q fits the qualitative sickle-cell defect
column7: P and Q cannot be inherited because mature red cells lack nuclei
column9:
Answer: (C) Quantitative thalassaemia versus qualitative sickle-cell change.
Why: A reduction in the amount of a globin-chain type changes the balance of haemoglobin-chain production, the quantitative distinction emphasised for thalassaemia. The stated structural substitution and oxygen-dependent sickling in Q fit a qualitative haemoglobin defect. The absence of nuclei in mature red cells does not prevent inherited instructions in their precursor lineage from determining which proteins those cells contain. Amount and molecular structure are therefore separate dimensions of an inherited protein disorder.
Why not the others: (A) reverses quantitative and qualitative effects. (B) ignores the stated inherited globin-production and sequence mechanisms. (D) confuses the mature cell's structure with the genome of the organism and its blood-cell precursors.
Key point: Ask whether an inherited protein defect changes how much is made or the properties of the molecule made.
column10: Globin-chain amount distinguished from a structural variant's oxygen-dependent effect
column11: Principles of inheritance and variation: Genetic Disorders; Thalassaemia; Sickle-Cell Anaemia

column3: Three dated specimens have measured cranial volumes: an older Homo erectus specimen, 900 cm3; a later Neanderthal specimen, 1400 cm3; and a still later Homo sapiens specimen, 1350 cm3. Separately, human and whale forelimbs share corresponding skeletal elements despite different uses, whereas bird and insect wings share flight function without the same underlying construction. Which pair of conclusions is supported?
column4: Brain volume must increase strictly in chronological order; all flight structures establish recent common ancestry
column5: The sample volumes prove a direct ancestor-descendant chain; different forelimb functions exclude homology
column6: The largest-brained specimen must be the ancestor of both others; bird and insect wings are homologous because both fly
column7: These sample volumes do not form a strictly increasing sequence; corresponding human-whale forelimb elements support homology despite functional divergence
column9:
Answer: (D) No strict sample-volume increase, and skeletal correspondence supports homology.
Why: The Neanderthal-to-later-sapiens comparison decreases from 1400 to 1350 cm3 in the stated measurements, so a strictly increasing volume rule fails for these samples. Relative dates and one measurement do not by themselves establish a direct ancestral chain or a universal progress ladder. In the anatomical comparison, correspondence of underlying forelimb elements supports common structural ancestry despite changed use. Flight alone supplies a functional resemblance between bird and insect wings, not the same evidence of structural homology. The volumes are supplied specimen observations, not claims that every individual in a named group had one fixed cranial capacity.
Why not the others: (A) contradicts the final measured decrease and equates a shared function with recent ancestry. (B) infers a lineage directly from three measurements and mistakes divergent function for absence of homology. (C) uses brain magnitude to reverse or invent ancestry and substitutes functional analogy for construction-based evidence.
Key point: Keep chronological evidence, a measured trait and homologous structural correspondence as distinct lines of evolutionary reasoning.
column10: A nonmonotone hominin specimen series is interpreted separately from homology and functional analogy
column11: Evolution: Origin and Evolution of Man; Evidence for Evolution

column3: A joint allows movement in several planes, including rotation, as at the shoulder. In a separate joint preparation, uric-acid crystals accompany inflammation while directly stimulated muscle fibres retain force. Which joint-type and disorder-mechanism pairing is most consistent?
column5: Hinge articulation; loss of bone mass defining osteoporosis
column6: Gliding articulation; autoimmune failure of the neuromuscular junction
column7: Fixed fibrous articulation; absence of actin in every muscle fibre
column9:
Answer: (A) Ball-and-socket articulation and gout-related inflammation.
Why: A ball-and-socket joint permits the stated multiaxial movement and rotation, unlike a simple hinge. Uric-acid crystal deposition with joint inflammation is the relevant mechanism for gout in the comparison. Preserved force after direct stimulation also separates joint-limited movement from a necessary intrinsic failure of all contractile machinery. These findings address different levels: articulation geometry and an inflammatory limitation of movement.
Why not the others: (B) limits the movement to a hinge pattern and substitutes decreased bone mass for the crystal evidence. (C) assigns a limited gliding joint to the shoulder-like movement and a different autoimmune target to the inflammation. (D) contradicts both the observed joint mobility and the retained muscle force.
Key point: Distinguish joint geometry and joint inflammation from defects of bone amount or muscle activation.
column10: Multiaxial joint geometry and urate evidence distinguish a joint disorder from muscle failure
column11: Locomotion and movement: Joints; Disorders of Muscular and Skeletal System

column3: A detergent disperses a phospholipid preparation into smaller aggregates without producing new covalent molecular species. In separate tubes, amylase produces smaller carbohydrate products from starch and a protease produces smaller peptide products from a protein. Which change is specifically physical dispersion rather than the stated covalent hydrolysis?
column4: The protease reaction, because all peptide bonds are noncovalent
column5: The amylase reaction, because starch is not a biomacromolecule
column6: Both enzyme reactions, because catalysts cannot alter chemical bonds
column7: The detergent-induced redistribution of intact phospholipid molecules
column9:
Answer: (D) Redistribution of intact phospholipid molecules.
Why: The detergent result changes how existing lipid molecules associate, while the stem explicitly excludes new covalent species. The enzyme results instead include smaller covalently connected products produced by hydrolysing glycosidic or peptide linkages. Catalysts can accelerate bond-changing reactions without being permanently consumed; their catalytic status does not make those reactions physical mixing.
Why not the others: (A) wrongly calls peptide bonds noncovalent. (B) denies starch's polymeric carbohydrate nature and ignores the stated hydrolysis products. (C) confuses catalyst conservation with conservation of every substrate bond.
Key point: Use evidence for changed covalent species to distinguish chemical breakdown from altered aggregation.
column10: Intact lipid redistribution distinguished from carbohydrate and peptide hydrolysis
column11: Biomolecules: Polysaccharides; Proteins; Lipids; Chemical Composition

column3: The cereal embryo in the figure has a single large lateral structure R and two protective sheaths P and Q at opposite ends of its embryonal axis. Which assignment correctly identifies P around the plumule, Q around the radicle and R?
column4: P coleorhiza; Q coleoptile; R endosperm
column5: P coleoptile; Q coleorhiza; R scutellum
column6: P scutellum; Q endosperm; R coleoptile
column7: P endosperm; Q scutellum; R coleorhiza
column9:
Answer: (B) Coleoptile, coleorhiza and scutellum.
Why: In the cereal embryo, the shoot-associated plumule is enclosed by the coleoptile, while the radicle is enclosed by the coleorhiza. The single lateral cotyledon is the scutellum, distinct from the surrounding nutritive endosperm. Reading the sheaths relative to the two embryonal-axis ends prevents exchanging their names simply because both are protective structures.
Why not the others: (A) swaps the two sheaths and calls the lateral embryonic cotyledon endosperm. (C) places a cotyledon and storage tissue where the two protective sheaths are shown. (D) again replaces axis-associated embryonic structures with the wrong tissue identities.
Key point: Identify cereal-embryo structures by their position and developmental identity, not merely by a shared protective or storage role.
column10: Cereal embryo geometry separates two protective sheaths from its lateral cotyledon
column11: Morphology of flowering plants: The Seed; Monocotyledonous Seed
